rv.q: There’s scarcely a superfluous word in this extraordinary piece.
This is a spellbinding evening that thrives on overturning assumptions, in line with the mountaineer’s perspective that scoffs at the madness of living a normal life.
It makes a play about imaginative as well as physical endurance.

The ensuing nightmare becomes vividly believable. Your heart is in your mouth as Josh Williams and Angus Yellowlees clamber across this perilous terrain; more importantly still, you empathise with them as they confront an impossible moral dilemma.
Their breathlessly exciting production, first staged at Bristol Old Vic, conjures wide-open landscapes and vertiginous drops.
Well, playwright David Greig and director Tom Morris have found a pretty damn good answer.
The ultimate lesson of this production is that you can do anything in the theatre as long as you rely on the audience’s willing imagination.
The production, which opened the renovated Bristol Old Vic in 2018, and comes to the West End after a UK tour, is majestically tense.
Overall it’s a robust and enjoyable evening.
The eschewing of naturalism is the key to the production’s grip and success.
This play provides its own answer: to see shows like this that asks larger questions, too, about what drives us as human beings.
Some bits are vertiginously brilliant; others look and feel like drama school exercises.
But neither figure was present on the mountain so their talk feels like a distraction from the key drama.
Tom Morris' production is a heartfelt, nail-biting, and almost acrobatic spectacle.

cn.t: David Greig's adaptation and Tom Morris's production achieve the seemingly impossible, turning Joe Simpson's mountaineering memoir into spellbinding, visually inventive theatre that thrills despite the story's familiarity.
